lessons.title: A lecture excerpt on climate change

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Today, I want to focus on a concept that's often misunderstood: climate feedback loops.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: A feedback loop occurs when a change in one part of the climate system amplifies, or dampens, that very same change.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Take melting Arctic ice, for instance. As ice disappears, it reflects less sunlight, which warms the ocean further.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: That warming, in turn, melts even more ice — a textbook example of a positive feedback loop.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Now, not all feedback loops accelerate warming — some act as natural brakes on the system.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: For your next assignment, I'd like you to identify one negative feedback loop and explain its mechanism.

questions.prompt: What is the main topic of the lecture?
questions.explanation: The professor introduces and explains feedback loops throughout.

questions.prompt: What example does the professor give of a positive feedback loop?
options: Melting Arctic ice reflecting less sunlight
questions.answer: Melting Arctic ice reflecting less sunlight
questions.explanation: The professor describes ice melting and reducing reflected sunlight.

questions.prompt: In this context, what does 'amplifies' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Amplifies' means to increase or strengthen an effect.

questions.prompt: What is the next assignment?
options: Identify a negative feedback loop and explain it
questions.answer: Identify a negative feedback loop and explain it
questions.explanation: The professor assigns students to explain a negative feedback loop.

questions.prompt: All feedback loops accelerate warming.
